mount-fuji.story: Traveller, on a clear day you can see Mount Fuji about 100 km southwest of Tokyo, an active stratovolcano on Honshu with a summit elevation of 3,776.24 m. It is Japan’s highest mountain, the second-highest volcano on any Asian island after Mount Kerinci on Sumatra, and the seventh-highest peak of an island on Earth, with an exceptionally symmetrical cone covered in snow for about five months of the year. It is a Japanese cultural icon frequently depicted in art and photography and visited by sightseers, hikers, and mountain climbers, and it is one of Japan’s Three Holy Mountains along with Mount Tate and Mount Haku. It is a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and one of Japan’s Historic Sites, added to the World Heritage List as a Cultural Site on June 22, 2013, with 25 sites of cultural interest in its locality, including the Shinto shrine Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha.
mount-fuji.name: Mount Fuji

taiseki-ji.story: If you journey to the foothills of Mount Fuji in Kamijo, Fujinomiya, Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan, you will find Taiseki-ji, the administrative center of Nichiren Shoshu Buddhism. It was founded in 1290 by Nikkō Shōnin, one of Nichiren Daishonin’s senior disciples, on land donated by Daigyo Sonrei, commonly known as Nanjo Tokimitsu. As the home of the Dai Gohonzon, Nichiren Shoshu’s object of worship, it draws pilgrim believers from various countries, and its open grounds are open to the public for sightseeing, though its religious buildings are restricted only to registered believers. You can also appreciate its historically significant buildings and gardens, national cultural assets, and old weeping cherry trees that line its Tatchū Sando, the main path lined with lodging temples.
taiseki-ji.name: Taiseki-ji

aokigahara.story: As you travel to Aokigahara, you find a forest on the northwestern flank of Mount Fuji on Honshu, also known as the Sea of Trees, thriving on 30 square kilometres of hardened lava laid down by the last major eruption of Mount Fuji in 864 CE. Its western edge, where several caves fill with ice in winter, is a popular destination for tourists and school trips, and designated trails lead to the Narusawa Ice Cave, Fugaku Wind Cave and Lake Sai Bat Cave—three larger lava caves near Mount Fuji, with the ice cave frozen year-round. In parts of the forest, the dense growth and porous lava rock absorb sound, contributing to a sense of solitude that some visitors attribute to the forest. The forest has a historical reputation as a home to yūrei, and signs at the head of some trails urge suicidal visitors to think of their families and contact a suicide prevention association.
aokigahara.name: Aokigahara

mount-echizen-dake.story: As you travel south-east of Mount Fuji, you’ll find Mount Echizen-dake, a Japanese volcanic peak. Its summit rises 1,504 meters high in Susono City, Shizuoka, and it is the highest peak of the Mount Ashitaka lava dome. This extinct volcano erupted in the mid-Pleistocene epoch, about 100,000 years ago. It was also depicted on the 50-yen banknote of the 1938 issue.
mount-echizen-dake.name: Mount Echizen-dake

lake-yamanaka.story: Traveller, Lake Yamanaka—‘Lake in the Mountains’—lies in the village of Yamanakako in Yamanashi Prefecture near Mount Fuji. It is the largest of the Fuji Five Lakes in surface area and the highest in elevation, the third highest lake in Japan with a mean surface altitude of 980.5 metres, and the shallowest of the Fuji Five Lakes with a maximum water depth of 13.5 metres. Formed by lava flows from an ancient eruption of Mount Fuji, it is drained by the Sagami River and is the only one of the Fuji Five Lakes with a natural outflow. You can enjoy boating, fishing, water-skiing, windsurfing, sightseeing, and swimming; if the wind comes from the west, the lake provides a smooth lift for paragliding at Mount Myōjinyama, and small cabins and camping sites are available, while the lake is within the borders of Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park and was added to the World Heritage List in 2013 as part of the Fujisan Cultural Site.
lake-yamanaka.name: Lake Yamanaka

yamamiya-sengen-shrine.story: For a traveller, Yamamiya Sengen-jinja in Fujinomiya, Shizuoka, Japan, offers a shrine that uniquely lacks a honden and instead has only an altar, using a Kannabi. It was built on an axis to provide the best views of Mount Fuji, and its altar is a place where one can pray to Mount Fuji. Though its exact construction year is unknown, archaeological digs have found earthenware dating back to the 12th or 15th century, and historical documents claim it was the predecessor to Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha. In 2013, it was inscribed as part of the World Heritage Site "Fujisan, sacred place and source of artistic inspiration" for representing Mount Fuji's role as an object of worship.
yamamiya-sengen-shrine.name: Yamamiya Sengen Shrine

mount-muro-mount-fuji.story: Traveler, pause at the gentle northwestern foot of Mount Fuji and see Mount Ōmuro, one of the many extinct volcanoes there that looks like an independent peak. Its top holds a crater depression, and because there is no mountain trail and the summit is surrounded by forests, the view is poor. On its south side lies Aokigahara, dotted with wind holes such as Motosu Wind Cave, Omuro Wind Cave, and Kamukura Wind Cave; as a wildlife sanctuary and national park special protected area, it prohibits the collection of insects and wildflowers. From Lake Shoji, Mount Fuji appears to loom over and surround Mount Ōmuro, a view nicknamed “Kodaki-Fuji,” or “Fuji Cradling a Child.”
mount-muro-mount-fuji.name: Mount Ōmuro (Mount Fuji)
